common_name: Green Gage Plum (Reine Claude, Historic French Fine-Flavored Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Green Gage is partially self-fruitful but sets heavier crops with a nearby European plum pollinator, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. Green Gage, known in France as Reine Claude, is an ancient European plum predating the 1500s that was named in England after Sir William Gage, who introduced it there in the 1720s, and it has been prized ever since as one of the finest-flavored plums grown, favored by chefs and preserve-makers above almost any other variety. The small to medium round fruit ripens to a yellow-green, sometimes lightly blushed with red, and the golden, freestone flesh carries an extraordinarily rich, sweet, honeyed flavor with none of the tartness common in many other plums. Harvest when fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure and the skin's green tone has softened toward amber-yellow, since underripe Green Gage lacks the sugar concentration that makes the variety famous; use promptly, since the delicate, thin-skinned fruit bruises easily and does not store long.

common_name: Yellow Egg Plum (Large Egg-Shaped Heirloom Canning Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Yellow Egg is partially self-fruitful but sets heavier crops with a nearby European plum pollinator, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. Yellow Egg is an old heirloom plum grown for its large, distinctive, genuinely egg-shaped fruit, which ripens to a bright, waxy yellow and can rival a small chicken egg in both size and shape, an unmistakable variety in the orchard. The firm, meaty flesh holds up exceptionally well to canning and cooking, historically making it one of the preferred varieties for home preserving even though the somewhat tart, thick skin makes it less popular for fresh eating than sweeter dessert plums. Trees are vigorous and productive, and the firm fruit tolerates handling well, making Yellow Egg a practical choice for home orchardists focused on putting up jams, canned plums, and baked goods rather than fresh snacking.

common_name: French Prune Plum (Prune d'Agen, Classic Drying Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; French Prune is self-fertile and well adapted to zones 5-9, including reasonably good performance in mild-winter Gulf Coast climates.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; self-fertile, so a single tree will produce fruit, though a nearby pollinator can increase yields. French Prune, known in its native France as Prune d'Agen, is the historic variety behind essentially the entire California and worldwide dried-prune industry, prized for exceptionally high natural sugar content that allows the small to medium, deep purple-blue oval fruit to be dried whole, pit and all, into the classic wrinkled prune without added sugar or elaborate processing. Fresh off the tree the rich, sweet, dense flesh is also excellent for eating out of hand, baking, and preserves, though the variety's fame rests on its drying quality. Harvest when fruit is fully ripe and soft, since sugar content peaks at full ripeness; for drying, halve or leave whole and dehydrate at low heat until leathery and shelf-stable.

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; President is self-fertile but benefits from a nearby European plum pollinator, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. President is a classic English European plum valued for ripening notably late in the season, well after most other plums have finished, which extends the fresh plum harvest into early fall for home orchards growing several varieties. The large, deep purple-blue fruit has firm, greenish-yellow flesh with a good sweet-tart balance, holding its texture and quality well both for fresh eating and for cooking and preserves. The tree is reliably productive and the firm-fleshed fruit keeps and handles better than many earlier, softer-fleshed plum varieties, making President a practical choice for gardeners who want to stretch the plum season and have fruit that travels well from tree to kitchen.

common_name: Empress Plum (Large Late-Season Purple European Plum)

planting.note: Plant bare-root while dormant in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Empress is self-fertile but benefits from a nearby European plum pollinator, and is best adapted to zones 5-8.

directions: Plant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, and prune annually to an open-center form. Empress is an English European plum grown for very large, deep purple fruit with firm, sweet, richly flavored flesh, ripening late in the season alongside President and extending a home orchard's plum harvest well past the peak of earlier varieties. The substantial fruit size and firm texture make Empress a good all-purpose plum, equally suited to fresh eating, baking, and preserving, and the tree is a dependable, consistent bearer once established. Thin fruit if the tree sets an especially heavy crop, since overloaded branches can break under the weight of large plums, and harvest once fruit yields slightly to gentle pressure and has fully colored for the best flavor.
